endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: To mitigate this risk, these test results can be combined with imaging/ lab tests as applicable for the specific cancer type.

evidence.title: Concordance of AI-driven antimicrobial recommendations using rapid molecular versus phenotypic-optimized workflows for bloodstream infections: a prospective study in a resource-limited setting
evidence.outcome: Therapeutic recommendation concordance of molecular-AI versus phenotypic-AI optimized workflow
evidence.effect: Therapeutic concordance 81.4% (192/236; κ=0.55). Resistance discordance predicted therapeutic discordance (aOR 7.70). Phenotypic optimization ensured 100% appropriate therapy.
evidence.quote: The integrated strategy delivered appropriate therapy 33 hours earlier in 81.4% of cases without requiring adjustment, with phenotypic optimization ensuring 100% appropriate therapy.

evidence.title: Diagnostic performance with and without artificial intelligence assistance in real-world screening mammography
evidence.outcome: Supplementary ultrasound detection of cancers missed by AI and mammography interpretation
evidence.effect: Supplementary ultrasound identified suspicious lesions in 9 cancers missed by both AI-CAD and radiologists on mammography. All 9 patients had dense breasts; ultrasound-guided biopsies established the diagnoses.
evidence.quote: All of these 9 patients had dense breasts, and subsequent ultrasound examinations revealed suspicious lesions, which were then diagnosed through ultrasound-guided biopsies.

evidence.title: Improving structural heart disease screening: AI-ECG and novice AI-guided focused cardiac ultrasound
evidence.outcome: Positive and negative predictive values of sequential AI-ECG and AI-FoCUS screening
evidence.effect: AI-ECG alone: PPV 29.6%, NPV 95.8%; positive AI-ECG followed by AI-FoCUS: PPV/NPV 96.1%/95.6%, with FoCUS imaging limited to 47%.
evidence.quote: A two-step strategy (positive AI-ECG followed by AI-FoCUS) maintained high PPV/NPV (96.1%/95.6%) but limited FoCUS imaging to 47%.

evidence.title: Direct deep learning analysis of three-dimensional automated breast ultrasound videos with reading mode optimization for breast cancer diagnosis
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic performance of human-AI integration vs standalone AI
evidence.effect: Experienced radiologists assisted by DL-3DABUV achieved significantly higher AUC (0.90 vs 0.82), sensitivity (90.5%-91.7% vs 82.1%), and specificity (92.0% vs 81.5%) than DL-3DABUV alone (all P<0.01).
evidence.quote: Experienced radiologists achieved significantly better diagnostic performance in both second-reading and concurrent-reading modes compared with DL-3DABUV alone (all P<0.01 for AUC, sensitivity, and specificity; Table 1 and Supplementary Table 1 ).
evidence.sample_unit: patients (test set; 547 total, read by 6 radiologists)

evidence.title: External validation of a commercial AI system for pulmonary embolism detection on chest CTPA: a multicenter study
evidence.effect: Combined had 7 errors (2 FN, 5 FP), reported as 75.9% reduction vs AI alone and radiologists alone; AI alone had 43 errors, manual 29.
evidence.quote: The combined radiologist + AI approach resulted in only 7 diagnostic errors (2 false-negative and 5 false-positive cases), representing a 75.9% reduction in errors compared to AI alone and a 75.9% reduction compared to radiologists alone.

evidence.title: Diagnostic performance with and without artificial intelligence assistance in real-world screening mammography
evidence.outcome: Cancers missed by standalone AI-CAD and detected by supplementary ultrasound
evidence.effect: AI-CAD missed 10/29 cancers (34%). Of these, 9 were also rated BI-RADS 1–2 by radiologists and were detected by same-day supplementary ultrasound.
evidence.quote: All of these 9 patients had dense breasts, and subsequent ultrasound examinations revealed suspicious lesions, which were then diagnosed through ultrasound-guided biopsies.

evidence.title: Utilizing large language models for detecting hospital-acquired conditions: an empirical study on pulmonary embolism
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Positive predictive value of LLM detection of pulmonary embolism adverse event at 0.4% prevalence
evidence.effect: High sensitivity (87.5-100%) and specificity (94.9-98.9%) but low PPV; best F1 was 28.11%, so LLMs cannot be relied on solely for definitive identification.
evidence.quote: While these models serve as effective screening tools to exclude non-PEAE cases, their lower PPV indicates they cannot be relied upon solely for definitive PEAE identification.

evidence.title: Performance of ChatGPT-5 in Diagnosing Fractures on Proximal Humerus and Intertrochanteric Femur X-Rays
evidence.outcome: False-positive fracture detection by AI on normal hip radiographs
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-5 had 16.7% specificity in IT femur fractures and frequently hallucinated fractures in normal hip X-rays.
evidence.quote: While it identified major fracture patterns and comminution reliably, it frequently hallucinated fractures in normal hip X-rays and missed fine details such as lesser tuberosity fragments and dislocations.

commentary.bottom_line: Four studies, two in real deployments, suggest that pairing AI diagnostic output with additional imaging, laboratory testing, or clinician review may catch errors that AI alone misses, including 9 breast cancers found by supplementary ultrasound after both AI and radiologists missed them. None of the studies were randomized, two were offline reader studies, and none reported outcomes for underserved populations.

perspectives.view: All four tests point the same direction, but none is randomized. The two real-deployment studies are prospective or quasi-experimental, and the breast study rests on 9 cancers. The two reader studies compare radiologists plus AI against AI alone rather than AI plus added tests, which makes them indirect. Consistency supports low certainty, while imprecision and indirectness limit it.

Standalone AI-CAD missed 10 of 29 cancers (34%), and same-day ultrasound found 9 of them. In pulmonary embolism CT review, AI alone made 43 errors and the combined read made 7. Other hazard studies report a best F1 of 28.11% at 0.4% prevalence and 16.7% specificity for hip fractures, which suggests false positives are common when AI stands alone.

In a live bloodstream infection workflow, molecular-AI and phenotypic-AI recommendations agreed in 81.4% of episodes (κ=0.55). Resistance discordance predicted therapeutic discordance (aOR 7.70), and phenotypic confirmation was reported to ensure appropriate therapy in all cases. This suggests discordance itself may serve as a trigger for confirmatory testing. The two reader studies ran offline, so their workflow fidelity is unknown.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide frames this practice as optional, stating that results "can be combined" with imaging or laboratory tests for the specific cancer type. The guide offers no threshold for when combination is required, so health systems would need to set local rules for which AI outputs require confirmation.

The breast study screened 2,061 examinations with supplementary ultrasound and found 9 additional cancers, all in women with dense breasts. No study reported staffing time, added test costs, or the rate of extra biopsies from false-positive confirmatory tests. Administrators therefore have no cost data to judge the burden of routine confirmation at scale.

In each tested workflow a clinician or a confirmatory test stood between the AI output and the diagnosis, and biopsies confirmed the cancers that ultrasound flagged. No study measured patient experience, delays from added testing, or how results were explained to patients.

commentary.research_gap: No randomized or cluster-randomized trial compares AI-alone diagnosis with AI plus protocolized confirmatory imaging or laboratory testing on patient outcomes, added costs, false-positive workups, or time to treatment. Studies also do not define which AI outputs or discordance patterns should trigger confirmation.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The studies came from South Korea, China, and one unreported setting, so it is unknown whether access to supplementary imaging or laboratory confirmation is feasible or equally protective in under-resourced U.S. settings, where these added tests may be harder to obtain.
